section.title: Derivatives and integrals of vector-valued functions

introduction.p: made \mathbf r(t) a position record. A position record becomes useful when we compare nearby times. The difference \mathbf r(t+h)-\mathbf r(t) is a displacement. Dividing by h gives average velocity over a short time interval.
Then the old single-variable idea returns: let the time interval shrink.

subsection.title: Velocity from a difference quotient
subsection.p: A small drone flies through a warehouse. Its position, in meters, is \mathbf r(t)=\left(t,\;t^2,\;3-\frac{t}{2}\right), where t is measured in seconds.

At t=1, \mathbf r(1)=\left(1,1,\frac52\right). At time 1+h, \mathbf r(1+h)=\left(1+h,\;(1+h)^2,\;3-\frac{1+h}{2}\right). The displacement from t=1 to t=1+h is
\mathbf r(1+h)-\mathbf r(1) \amp= \left(h,\;(1+h)^2-1,\;-\frac{h}{2}\right) \amp= \left(h,\;2h+h^2,\;-\frac{h}{2}\right).
The average velocity over that interval is \frac{\mathbf r(1+h)-\mathbf r(1)}{h}=\left(1,\;2+h,\;-\frac12\right). Letting h\to0, we get the instantaneous velocity at t=1: \left(1,2,-\frac12\right).
This vector points in the direction the drone is moving at that instant.

exercise.title: Why does \mathbf r'(t) point along the path?

statement.p: Suppose \mathbf r'(t)\ne\mathbf0. The derivative is a limit of difference quotients \frac{\mathbf r(t+h)-\mathbf r(t)}{h}. Each numerator \mathbf r(t+h)-\mathbf r(t) is a displacement vector connecting two nearby points on the curve. As h\to 0^+, what happens to the direction of that displacement vector, and why does this explain that \mathbf r'(t) ends up pointing along the path rather than off in some other direction?

hint.p: Picture the two points \mathbf r(t) and \mathbf r(t+h) sliding toward each other as h shrinks. The chord between them is a secant of the curve; think about what a secant becomes in the limit. Dividing by the positive number h only rescales the vector, it does not turn it.

statement.p: The derivative of \mathbf r(t) at t=a is \boxed{\mathbf r'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathbf r(a+h)-\mathbf r(a)}{h}} when this limit exists.

subsection.p: When \mathbf r(t) is a position vector, the derivative \mathbf v(t)=\mathbf r'(t) is called the velocity. The derivative of velocity, \mathbf a(t)=\mathbf v'(t)=\mathbf r''(t), is called the acceleration.
For the drone, \mathbf r(t)=\left(t,\;t^2,\;3-\frac{t}{2}\right), so we expect \mathbf v(t)=\left(1,2t,-\frac12\right), and \mathbf a(t)=(0,2,0). We will justify the component-by-component rule next.

subsection.title: Differentiating component by component
subsection.p: A helix gives a clean example. Let \mathbf r(t)=\left(2\cos t,\;2\sin t,\;\frac{t}{3}\right). The component functions are x(t)=2\cos t,\qquad y(t)=2\sin t,\qquad z(t)=\frac{t}{3}. Differentiating each one gives x'(t)=-2\sin t, y'(t)=2\cos t, and z'(t)=\frac13. So \mathbf r'(t)=\left(-2\sin t,\;2\cos t,\;\frac13\right). At t=0, \mathbf r(0)=(2,0,0), and \mathbf r'(0)=\left(0,2,\frac13\right). The point is at the right side of the circle and is moving in the positive y-direction while also rising.

figure.caption: The derivative vector points tangent to the path. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p: The rule is exactly what the example showed.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=\bigl(r_1(t),r_2(t),\ldots,r_n(t)\bigr). Then \mathbf r'(a) exists if and only if each component derivative r_i'(a) exists. In that case, \boxed{\mathbf r'(a)=\bigl(r_1'(a),r_2'(a),\ldots,r_n'(a)\bigr).}

proof.p: Use the definition: \frac{\mathbf r(a+h)-\mathbf r(a)}{h}=\left(\frac{r_1(a+h)-r_1(a)}{h},\ldots,\frac{r_n(a+h)-r_n(a)}{h}\right). A vector limit exists exactly when all component limits exist. Those component limits are the ordinary derivatives r_i'(a).

subsection.p: The hypothesis that the component derivatives exist is real. A continuous curve can still fail to have a velocity.

example.title: A sharp corner has no velocity vector

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(|t|,t). This curve is continuous at t=0, but \frac{\mathbf r(h)-\mathbf r(0)}{h}=\left(\frac{|h|}{h},1\right). If h>0, this quotient is (1,1). If h<0, it is (-1,1). The two one-sided limits do not agree. Therefore \mathbf r'(0) does not exist.
Geometrically, the curve has a corner at the origin. The point arrives from one direction and leaves in another, so there is no single tangent velocity at that instant.

subsection.p: At endpoints of a time interval, we use the same caution as in single-variable calculus. A curve defined only for t\ge0 may have a right-hand velocity at t=0, but not a two-sided derivative there unless the curve is defined on both sides.

subsection.title: Tangent lines to a motion path
subsection.p: If \mathbf r'(a)\ne\mathbf 0, then the tangent line to the curve at time a is the line through \mathbf r(a) in the direction \mathbf r'(a). Thus \boxed{\mathbf L(s)=\mathbf r(a)+s\mathbf r'(a)} is a parametrization of the tangent line.

example.title: A tangent line to a drone path

statement.p: For \mathbf r(t)=\left(t,\;t^2,\;3-\frac{t}{2}\right), we found \mathbf r(1)=\left(1,1,\frac52\right) and \mathbf r'(1)=\left(1,2,-\frac12\right). So the tangent line at t=1 is \mathbf L(s)=\left(1,1,\frac52\right)+s\left(1,2,-\frac12\right). In coordinates, x=1+s,\qquad y=1+2s,\qquad z=\frac52-\frac{s}{2}.

subsection.p: The velocity vector gives the instantaneous direction of motion, not merely the direction of the curve as a set. If the same geometric curve is traced with a different clock, the velocity vector changes.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r_1(t)=(\cos t,\sin t) and \mathbf r_2(t)=(\cos 2t,\sin 2t). Both trace the unit circle. But \mathbf r_1'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t), while \mathbf r_2'(t)=(-2\sin 2t,2\cos 2t). The second velocity vector has twice the length. The same circle is being traced twice as fast.

subsection.p: The length of the velocity vector is the speed: \text{speed}=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|. Speed will become the key to arc length in .

exercise.title: What does the tangent vector's direction and length tell you?

statement.p: The tangent line at time a uses \mathbf r'(a) as its direction, so \mathbf r'(t) is tangent to the curve. Yet two motions can trace the very same curve while their velocity vectors differ in length, as the unit circle examples above showed. Explain in your own words why the direction of \mathbf r'(t) determines the tangent line to the curve, with its sign recording the chosen direction of travel, while the length \|\mathbf r'(t)\| is instead a feature of how the curve is being traced.

hint.p: Imagine driving along a fixed road. The road decides which way your car is pointing at each spot, but you choose how fast to go. Which of those two things is "direction" and which is "length"? Re-tracing the same circle twice as fast multiplies the velocity by a constant without rotating it.

subsection.title: Differentiation rules
subsection.p: Since derivatives are computed component by component, the familiar single-variable rules return almost unchanged.
Before listing them, here is one example.

example.title: A dot product changing with time

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2,0),\qquad \mathbf s(t)=(1,\cos t,\sin t). Then \mathbf r(t)\cdot\mathbf s(t)=t+t^2\cos t. Differentiating directly, \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf r(t)\cdot\mathbf s(t)\bigr)=1+2t\cos t-t^2\sin t.

Now compute using a product rule: \mathbf r'(t)=(1,2t,0), \mathbf s'(t)=(0,-\sin t,\cos t). Then
\mathbf r'(t)\cdot\mathbf s(t)+\mathbf r(t)\cdot\mathbf s'(t) \amp= (1,2t,0)\cdot(1,\cos t,\sin t) \amp\quad +(t,t^2,0)\cdot(0,-\sin t,\cos t) \amp= 1+2t\cos t-t^2\sin t.
The ordinary product rule is still there, but now it is written with dot products.

Suppose \mathbf r(t) and \mathbf s(t) are differentiable vector-valued functions, and f(t) is a differentiable real-valued function. Then \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf r+\mathbf s\bigr)=\mathbf r'+\mathbf s', \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(f\mathbf r\bigr)=f'\mathbf r+f\mathbf r', and \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s\bigr)=\mathbf r'\cdot\mathbf s+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s'. If \mathbf r(t) and \mathbf s(t) are functions into \mathbb R^3, then \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf r\times\mathbf s\bigr)=\mathbf r'\times\mathbf s+\mathbf r\times\mathbf s'.

proof.p:
Each rule follows by writing the vectors in components and applying the ordinary single-variable differentiation rules. The dot product rule, for example, is just the product rule applied to each term: \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s=r_1s_1+\cdots+r_ns_n. Then
\frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s) \amp= (r_1's_1+r_1s_1')+\cdots+(r_n's_n+r_ns_n') \amp= \mathbf r'\cdot\mathbf s+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s'.
The cross product rule is checked the same way from the component formula for \mathbf r\times\mathbf s.

subsection.p: The differentiability assumptions matter. If a component has a corner, as in |t|, then the corresponding vector function may fail to have a derivative, and the rules above have nothing to apply to at that time.

subsection.title: Integrating vector-valued functions
subsection.p: Differentiation takes us from position to velocity: \mathbf r(t)\longmapsto \mathbf r'(t). Integration goes the other way. It adds many tiny velocity vectors to recover a net displacement.

Suppose a drifting boat has velocity \mathbf v(t)=(2,\cos t,3t^2),\qquad 0\le t\le\pi. The displacement from t=0 to t=\pi is \int_0^\pi \mathbf v(t)\,dt. Compute component by component:
\int_0^\pi (2,\cos t,3t^2)\,dt \amp= \left(\int_0^\pi 2\,dt,\;\int_0^\pi \cos t\,dt,\;\int_0^\pi 3t^2\,dt\right) \amp= \left(2\pi,\;\sin t\bigg|_0^\pi,\;t^3\bigg|_0^\pi\right) \amp= (2\pi,0,\pi^3).
The boat's net displacement is (2\pi,0,\pi^3).

statement.p: If \mathbf v(t)=\bigl(v_1(t),v_2(t),\ldots,v_n(t)\bigr), then \boxed{\int_a^b \mathbf v(t)\,dt=\left(\int_a^b v_1(t)\,dt,\;\int_a^b v_2(t)\,dt,\;\ldots,\;\int_a^b v_n(t)\,dt\right)} whenever the component integrals exist.

subsection.p: For an indefinite integral, \int \mathbf v(t)\,dt means a vector-valued antiderivative: \mathbf R'(t)=\mathbf v(t). The constant of integration is now a constant vector.

exercise.title: What does integrating velocity recover, and why a whole vector \mathbf C?

statement.p: When you integrate a velocity \mathbf v(t), the result is again a vector. In words, what quantity does this integral recover, and how does that meaning explain why the constant of integration must be a whole vector \mathbf C rather than a single number? Think about what kind of information you must supply to pin down the actual motion.

hint.p: Antidifferentiating each component leaves one unknown number per component, and there is a separate one in each coordinate direction. What single object do you get when you collect (C_1,C_2,C_3) together? Geometrically, knowing the velocity tells you the shape of the trip but not where it began.

statement.p: Let \mathbf v(t)=(6t,\;e^t,\;\cos t). Then \int \mathbf v(t)\,dt=(3t^2,\;e^t,\;\sin t)+\mathbf C, where \mathbf C=(C_1,C_2,C_3) is a constant vector.

subsection.p: The condition that the component integrals exist is not decoration. If even one component fails to have an ordinary definite integral, then the vector integral fails.

example.title: One bad component breaks the vector integral

statement.p: The function \mathbf v(t)=\left(\frac1t,0\right) is not bounded near t=0. The ordinary integral \int_0^1 \frac1t\,dt does not exist as a finite definite integral. Therefore \int_0^1 \left(\frac1t,0\right)\,dt does not exist as an ordinary vector integral.
A vector integral is only as well behaved as its components.

subsection.title: The Fundamental Theorem for vector-valued functions
subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus now returns in vector form.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=\bigl(r_1(t),\ldots,r_n(t)\bigr) be differentiable on an interval, and suppose \mathbf r'(t) has continuous components on [a,b]. Then \boxed{\int_a^b \mathbf r'(t)\,dt=\mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a).}

proof.p:
Write \mathbf r'(t)=\bigl(r_1'(t),\ldots,r_n'(t)\bigr). Then
\int_a^b \mathbf r'(t)\,dt \amp= \left(\int_a^b r_1'(t)\,dt,\ldots,\int_a^b r_n'(t)\,dt\right) \amp= \left(r_1(b)-r_1(a),\ldots,r_n(b)-r_n(a)\right) \amp= \mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a).
The middle step is the single-variable Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, applied one component at a time.

subsection.p: The continuity assumption on the components of \mathbf r' is a friendly sufficient condition. It guarantees that the component integrals behave exactly as expected. There are more advanced versions with weaker hypotheses, but this one is the right tool for the curves in this course.

subsection.title: Initial value problems for motion
subsection.p: Often we know velocity or acceleration first, and we want position.

A basketball is thrown across a gym. Let the x-axis point across the court, the y-axis point sideways, and the z-axis point upward. Suppose the ball starts at \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,1) meters and has initial velocity \mathbf v(0)=(8,3,10) meters per second. Ignore air resistance. Then acceleration is constant: \mathbf a(t)=(0,0,-9.8).

Since \mathbf v'(t)=\mathbf a(t), we integrate acceleration: \mathbf v(t)=\int (0,0,-9.8)\,dt=(0,0,-9.8t)+\mathbf C. Use \mathbf v(0)=(8,3,10) to get \mathbf C=(8,3,10). Thus \mathbf v(t)=(8,3,10-9.8t).
Now integrate velocity: \mathbf r(t)=\int (8,3,10-9.8t)\,dt=(8t,3t,10t-4.9t^2)+\mathbf D. Use \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,1) to get \mathbf D=(0,0,1). Therefore \boxed{\mathbf r(t)=(8t,\;3t,\;1+10t-4.9t^2).}

The three coordinates tell three simpler stories: x(t)=8t, y(t)=3t, z(t)=1+10t-4.9t^2. The horizontal motion is linear. The vertical motion is the familiar falling-object parabola from single-variable calculus.

statement.p: A small underwater robot has velocity \mathbf v(t)=(1+t,\;2,\;e^{-t}) and starts at \mathbf r(0)=(3,-1,0). Find \mathbf r(t).

Since \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf v(t), we integrate: \mathbf r(t)=\left(t+\frac{t^2}{2},\;2t,\;-e^{-t}\right)+\mathbf C. Use the initial position: \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,-1)+\mathbf C=(3,-1,0). So \mathbf C=(3,-1,1). Therefore \boxed{\mathbf r(t)=\left(3+t+\frac{t^2}{2},\;-1+2t,\;1-e^{-t}\right).}

subsection.p: This is an initial value problem. The derivative information gives a family of possible motions. The initial condition chooses the one motion that actually starts in the given place.

Differentiation and integration now work for motion in space. But a subtle problem has appeared. The integral of velocity gives displacement, not distance traveled. A runner who completes one lap has \mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a)=\mathbf 0, but she certainly did not run zero meters. To measure distance traveled, we must add up tiny lengths \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. We return to this question in . First, the same curve derivatives let us revisit the surface grids from Chapter 4.

subsection.title: Velocities along a surface grid
subsection.p: In , we described a surface by \mathbf r(s,t) and drew its grid curves by holding one parameter fixed. We can now find the velocities along those curves. Each calculation uses an ordinary derivative of a function with just one changing input.

Choose an interior parameter pair (s_0,t_0), so that either parameter can vary a little in both directions. The two grid curves through P=\mathbf r(s_0,t_0) are \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=\mathbf r(s,t_0),\qquad \boldsymbol\beta(t)=\mathbf r(s_0,t). In the first curve t_0 is a constant; in the second s_0 is a constant. Their velocities at P are \boxed{\mathbf v=\boldsymbol\alpha'(s_0),\qquad \mathbf w=\boldsymbol\beta'(t_0).} A nonzero velocity is a tangent vector to its grid curve, based at P. The parameters need not measure physical time: velocity here means change of position per unit change of the parameter.

statement.p: For \mathbf r(s,t)=(s,t,s^2+t^2), freezing one input gives \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=(s,t_0,s^2+t_0^2),\qquad \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(s_0,t,s_0^2+t^2). Differentiate these one-variable functions component by component: \mathbf v=(1,0,2s_0),\qquad \mathbf w=(0,1,2t_0). The vectors cannot be parallel: their first two coordinates already give two independent directions. Their cross product is \mathbf v\times\mathbf w=(-2s_0,-2t_0,1), perpendicular to both grid-curve tangents and never zero.

definition.title: Regular parameter point and a normal vector

statement.p: Suppose the two grid-curve velocities exist at an interior pair (s_0,t_0). The parametrization is regular at this parameter point when the velocities are linearly independent, equivalently when \boxed{\mathbf v\times\mathbf w\ne\mathbf0.} When they are dependent, the parameter point is nonregular. Thus regularity is a property of the chosen parametrization at a parameter pair, not just a test on the coordinates of its image point.

For surface geometry we work with parametrizations whose grid-curve velocities exist nearby and vary continuously as the two parameters vary. At a regular point they span the tangent plane to the local surface sheet; a normal vector to this sheet at P is \boxed{\mathbf N=\mathbf v\times\mathbf w.} Any nonzero multiple of \mathbf N is also normal. Swapping the two velocities changes its sign. The cross-product rule proves perpendicularity to both grid tangents immediately; the full justification that their plane describes the local sheet is given in .

subsection.p: The nearby-continuity assumption rules out erratic behavior between the grid curves; two derivatives at a single pair alone do not control an entire surface. For the polynomial and trigonometric parametrizations here, the displayed velocity formulas vary continuously. On a surface that crosses itself, the normal belongs to the sheet selected by the parameter pair.

example.title: A grid that collapses at a cone vertex

statement.p: Consider \mathbf r(s,t)=(s\cos t,s\sin t,s),\qquad s,t\in\mathbb R. Its image is the double cone x^2+y^2=z^2. Positive and negative s describe its upper and lower halves. Both inputs can vary on either side of every chosen value, including s=0.

Freezing t=t_0 gives a straight grid line \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=(s\cos t_0,s\sin t_0,s). Freezing s=s_0 gives a circular grid curve \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(s_0\cos t,s_0\sin t,s_0). Their velocities are \mathbf v=(\cos t_0,\sin t_0,1),\qquad \mathbf w=(-s_0\sin t_0,s_0\cos t_0,0). Hence \boxed{\mathbf N=(-s_0\cos t_0,-s_0\sin t_0,s_0).} The parametrization is regular exactly when s_0\ne0. At (0,t_0), the circular grid curve is the constant curve \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(0,0,0), so \mathbf w=\mathbf0 and \mathbf N=\mathbf0. The zero vector supplies no normal direction.

For this cone the vertex really has no single tangent plane. The straight grid lines with t_0=0,\pi/2,\pi have velocities (1,0,1),(0,1,1),(-1,0,1). Their determinant is 2, so these three directions cannot lie in one plane. This geometric argument says more than merely observing a zero cross product.

figure.caption: Grid curves on the double cone. The blue straight grid line and orange circular grid curve meet at the regular point P; the arrows show their velocities \mathbf v,\mathbf w and a normal \mathbf N, scaled for visibility. At the red vertex O, the circular grid has collapsed to a point. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

image.shortdescription: Double cone with grid curves, tangent velocities and a normal at a regular point, and a red nonregular vertex.

subsection.p: A nonregular parametrization does not always mean that the image itself has a sharp point. For example, \mathbf q(s,t)=(s^3,t,0) covers the ordinary xy-plane. Its grid velocities at (s_0,t_0) are (3s_0^2,0,0) and (0,1,0), so their cross product vanishes when s_0=0. The first grid curve simply has zero velocity there. The same plane has the regular parametrization \widetilde{\mathbf q}(a,b)=(a,b,0), whose grid velocities are (1,0,0) and (0,1,0).

statement.p: For the bowl \mathbf r(s,t)=(s,t,s^2+t^2), write the two frozen-parameter grid curves through the parameter pair (1,-1). Find their velocities and a normal at the image point. Is the parametrization regular there? What happens to the normal if the two velocities are exchanged?

hint.p: In one curve set t=-1; in the other set s=1. Differentiate each curve in its remaining variable, then use the cross product.

solution.p: The curves are \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=(s,-1,s^2+1) and \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(1,t,1+t^2). At P=(1,-1,2) their velocities are (1,0,2) and (0,1,-2). Their cross product (-2,2,1) is nonzero, so the parameter point is regular and this vector is normal. Exchanging the velocities gives the opposite normal (2,-2,-1).

subsection.p: The ordinary derivatives of two grid curves have given us two tangent directions and, at regular points, a normal. will collect the same velocities in a matrix and explain their role in a local linear approximation. We next return to a single moving point and measure its speed and distance traveled.
